chapters.title: 25. How the Procurator Tried to Save Judas from Kiriath
paragraphs: The darkness that had come from the Mediterranean Sea covered the city the procurator hated. The suspension bridges joining the temple to the dreadful Antonia Tower vanished; an abyss came down from the sky and flooded the winged gods above the hippodrome, the Hasmonean palace with its loopholes, the bazaars, the caravanserais, the lanes, the pools... Yershalaim was gone—the great city—as if it had never existed in the world. The darkness devoured everything, and it frightened every living thing in Yershalaim and its surroundings. The strange cloud had been brought in from the sea toward the end of the day, the fourteenth day of the spring month of Nisan.

It had already lowered its belly onto the Bald Skull, where the executioners were hastily stabbing the men being executed; it lowered itself onto the temple in Yershalaim, crept down from its hill in smoky streams and flooded the Lower City. It poured in at the windows and drove people from the crooked streets into their houses. It was in no hurry to give up its moisture and gave up only light. Whenever fire ripped open the black, smoky brew, the great bulk of the temple with its glittering covering of scales flew up out of the pitch darkness. But the fire went out in an instant, and the temple sank into the dark abyss. Several times it rose up out of it and fell back again, and each time its fall was accompanied by the crash of catastrophe.

Other tremulous flickers called up from the abyss the palace of Herod the Great, which faced the temple from the western hill, and its dreadful eyeless golden statues flew up toward the black sky, stretching out their arms to it. But again the heavenly fire hid itself, and heavy blows of thunder drove the golden idols back into the dark.

The downpour came suddenly, and then the storm turned into a hurricane. In the very spot where, around noon, near the marble bench in the garden, the procurator and the high priest had talked, a cypress snapped like a cane, with a crack like a cannon shot. Along with the spray and the hail, torn-off roses, magnolia leaves, small branches and sand were swept onto the balcony under the columns. The hurricane was ravaging the garden.
At that time there was only one person under the columns, and that person was the procurator.

He was no longer sitting in the chair but reclining on a couch beside a small low table laden with food and with wine in jugs. Another couch, empty, stood on the other side of the table. At the procurator’s feet spread a red puddle, as if of blood, that no one had wiped up, and the shards of a broken jug lay scattered about. The servant who had been laying the table for the procurator before the storm had for some reason lost his head under his gaze and grown flustered at having displeased him in some way, and the procurator, growing angry with him, had smashed the jug on the mosaic floor, saying:
“Why don’t you look me in the face when you serve? Have you stolen something?”

The African’s black face turned gray, mortal terror appeared in his eyes, he trembled and very nearly broke the second jug as well, but the procurator’s anger for some reason flew away as quickly as it had flown in. The African rushed to pick up the shards and wipe up the puddle, but the procurator waved him off, and the slave ran away. And the puddle remained.

Now, during the hurricane, the African was hiding by the niche that held the statue of a white naked woman with a bowed head, afraid of showing himself at the wrong moment and at the same time afraid of missing the moment when the procurator might call him.

Reclining on the couch in the stormy half-dark, the procurator poured wine into his cup himself and drank it in long draughts; now and then he touched the bread, crumbled it and swallowed it in small pieces; from time to time he sucked out an oyster, chewed a lemon and drank again.

If it had not been for the roar of the water, if it had not been for the thunderclaps that seemed to threaten to flatten the palace roof, if it had not been for the rattle of the hail hammering on the balcony steps, one might have heard that the procurator was muttering something, talking to himself. And if the unsteady flickering of the heavenly fire had turned into a steady light, an observer could have seen that the procurator’s face, with eyes inflamed by the sleepless nights of late and by wine, expressed impatience; that the procurator was not only looking at the two white roses drowned in the red puddle but kept turning his face toward the garden, into the spray and the sand; that he was waiting for someone, waiting impatiently.

Some time passed, and the veil of water before the procurator’s eyes began to thin. Furious as the hurricane was, it was weakening. Branches no longer cracked and fell. The thunderclaps and flashes came less often. What floated over Yershalaim now was no longer a violet coverlet trimmed with white but an ordinary gray rearguard cloud. The storm was being carried off toward the Dead Sea.

Now one could already make out, each on its own, the noise of the rain and the noise of the water pouring down the gutters and straight down the steps of the staircase by which the procurator had gone that afternoon to announce the sentence in the square. And at last the fountain, drowned out until then, could be heard as well. It was growing lighter. Blue windows appeared in the gray veil that was fleeing eastward.

Then from far away, breaking through the patter of the now quite feeble little rain, faint sounds of trumpets and the clatter of several hundred hooves reached the procurator’s ears. Hearing this, the procurator stirred, and his face came alive. The ala was returning from Bald Mountain. Judging by the sound, it was passing through the very square where the sentence had been announced.

At last the procurator heard the long-awaited footsteps as well, and a slapping on the stairs that led up to the upper terrace of the garden, right in front of the balcony. The procurator stretched out his neck, and his eyes shone, expressing joy.

Between two marble lions there appeared first a hooded head and then a man soaked through, in a cloak clinging to his body. It was the very man who before the sentence had whispered with the procurator in a darkened room of the palace, and who during the execution had sat on a three-legged stool, playing with a twig.
Paying no heed to the puddles, the man in the hood crossed the garden terrace, stepped onto the mosaic floor of the balcony and, raising his hand, said in a high, pleasant voice:
“Health and joy to the procurator!” The newcomer spoke in Latin.
“Gods!” exclaimed Pilate. “Why, there isn’t a dry thread on you! What a hurricane! Eh? I beg you, come inside at once. Change your clothes, do me that kindness.”

The newcomer threw back his hood, revealing a head soaked through, with hair plastered to his forehead, and, with a polite smile on his shaven face, began to decline the change of clothes, assuring him that a little rain could do him no harm whatsoever.

“I won’t hear of it,” Pilate answered, and clapped his hands. With this he summoned the servants who were hiding from him and told them to take care of the newcomer and then to serve the hot dish at once. The procurator’s visitor needed very little time to dry his hair, change his clothes and his shoes and generally put himself in order, and he soon appeared on the balcony in dry sandals, in a dry crimson military cloak, and with his hair smoothed down.

By this time the sun had come back to Yershalaim and, before going away to drown in the Mediterranean Sea, was sending farewell rays to the city the procurator hated and gilding the balcony steps. The fountain had come fully back to life and was singing with all its might; the doves had come out onto the sand, cooing, hopping over the broken branches and pecking at something in the wet sand. The red puddle had been wiped up, the shards cleared away, and meat was steaming on the table.
“I am ready to hear the procurator’s orders,” said the newcomer, coming up to the table.
“But you will hear none until you sit down and drink some wine,” Pilate answered courteously, and pointed to the other couch.

The newcomer reclined, and a servant poured thick red wine into his cup. Another servant, bending carefully over Pilate’s shoulder, filled the procurator’s cup. After this the procurator dismissed both servants with a gesture.

While the newcomer ate and drank, Pilate, sipping his wine, kept glancing at his guest through narrowed eyes. The man who had come to Pilate was middle-aged, with a very pleasant, round, tidy face and a fleshy nose. His hair was of some indeterminate color. Now, as it dried, it was growing lighter. It would have been hard to establish the visitor’s nationality. The main thing that defined his face was perhaps its expression of good nature, which was spoiled, however, by his eyes, or rather not by his eyes but by the visitor’s manner of looking at the person he was talking to. Usually the visitor kept his small eyes under half-lowered, somewhat odd, as if slightly swollen lids. Then a harmless slyness glimmered in the slits of those eyes. One must suppose that the procurator’s guest was inclined to humor. But at times, banishing that glinting humor from the slits entirely, the procurator’s present guest would open his lids wide and look at the person he was talking to suddenly and point-blank, as if to make out quickly some barely noticeable speck on the other man’s nose. This lasted an instant, after which the lids lowered again, the slits narrowed, and good nature and a sly intelligence began to glimmer in them once more.
The newcomer did not refuse a second cup of wine either; with visible pleasure he swallowed several oysters, tasted the boiled vegetables and ate a piece of meat.
When he had eaten his fill, he praised the wine:
“An excellent vine, Procurator, but this is not ‘Falerno’?”
“‘Caecuba,’ thirty years old,” the procurator responded courteously.

The guest put his hand to his heart, declined to eat anything more, and declared that he had had enough. Then Pilate filled his cup, and the guest did the same. Both diners poured a little wine from their cups onto the dish of meat, and the procurator said loudly, raising his cup:
“To us, to you, Caesar, father of the Romans, the dearest and best of men!”

After this they drank their wine to the end, and the Africans cleared the food from the table, leaving the fruit and the jugs on it. Once again the procurator dismissed the servants with a gesture and remained alone with his guest under the colonnade.
“And so,” Pilate began quietly, “what can you tell me about the mood in this city?”
Involuntarily he turned his gaze to where, beyond the terraces of the garden, down below, the colonnades and the flat roofs, gilded by the last rays, were burning out.
“I believe, Procurator,” the guest answered, “that the mood in Yershalaim is now satisfactory.”
“So one can vouch that disorders no longer threaten?”
“One can vouch,” the guest answered, looking kindly at the procurator, “for only one thing in the world—the might of the great Caesar.”
“May the gods send him long life,” Pilate took up at once, “and universal peace.” He was silent for a moment and went on: “So you believe the troops can now be withdrawn?”
“I believe the cohort of the Lightning can leave,” the guest answered, and added: “It would be a good thing if it paraded through the city by way of farewell.”

“A very good idea,” the procurator approved. “The day after tomorrow I shall let it go and leave myself, and—I swear to you by the feast of the twelve gods, I swear by the Lares—I would give a great deal to be doing it today!”
“The procurator does not like Yershalaim?” the guest asked good-naturedly.

“Have mercy,” the procurator exclaimed, smiling, “there is no more hopeless place on earth. I am not even speaking of the land itself! I fall ill every time I have to come here. But that would be only half the trouble. But these feasts—magi, sorcerers, wizards, these flocks of pilgrims... Fanatics, fanatics! That messiah alone, whom they suddenly took it into their heads to expect this year—what that cost us! Every minute you are waiting to find yourself a witness to the most unpleasant bloodshed. Forever shuffling troops about, reading denunciations and slanders, half of which, what is more, are written about you yourself! You must agree that it is tedious. Oh, if it were not for the imperial service!..”
“Yes, the feasts here are difficult,” the guest agreed.

“I wish with all my heart that they were over soon,” Pilate added vigorously. “I shall at last be able to go back to Caesarea. Would you believe it, this delirious structure of Herod’s”—the procurator waved his hand along the colonnade, so that it was clear he was speaking of the palace—“is positively driving me mad. I cannot spend the night in it. The world has never known stranger architecture!.. Yes, but let us return to business. First of all, that cursed Bar-Rabban is not troubling you?”

Here the guest sent his peculiar look at the procurator’s cheek. But the procurator was gazing into the distance with bored eyes, his face wrinkled in distaste, contemplating the part of the city that lay at his feet, fading in the early evening. The guest’s look faded too, and his lids lowered.
“One must suppose that Bar has now become as harmless as a lamb,” the guest began, and little wrinkles appeared on his round face. “It would be awkward for him to rebel now.”
“Too famous?” asked Pilate with a faint smile.
“The procurator, as always, grasps the matter with great subtlety!”
“But in any case,” the procurator remarked anxiously, and a long, thin finger with the black stone of a ring rose upward, “it will be necessary...”
“Oh, the procurator may be sure that as long as I am in Judea, Bar will not take a single step without someone following at his heels.”
“Now I am at ease—as, indeed, I always am when you are here.”
“The procurator is too kind!”
“And now I ask you to report to me on the execution,” said the procurator.
“What exactly interests the procurator?”
“Were there no attempts on the part of the crowd to express indignation? That is the main thing, of course.”
“None,” the guest answered.
“Very good. Did you establish yourself that death had come?”
“The procurator may be sure of it.”
“And tell me... were they given the drink before they were hung on the posts?”
“Yes. But he”—here the guest closed his eyes—“refused to drink it.”
“Who exactly?” asked Pilate.
“Forgive me, hegemon!” the guest exclaimed. “Did I not name him? Ha-Notsri.”
“Madman!” said Pilate, grimacing for some reason. A vein began to twitch under his left eye. “To die of burns from the sun! Why refuse what is offered by law? In what words did he refuse?”
“He said,” the guest answered, again closing his eyes, “that he was grateful, and did not blame them for taking his life.”
“Whom?” Pilate asked hollowly.
“That, hegemon, he did not say.”
“Did he not try to preach anything in the presence of the soldiers?”
“No, hegemon, he was not wordy this time. The only thing he said was that among the human vices he considered cowardice one of the very chief.”
“What was that said for?” the guest heard a voice that had suddenly cracked.
“That was impossible to understand. In general he behaved strangely—as, indeed, he always did.”
“What was strange about it?”
“He kept trying to look into the eyes of one or another of the people around him, and he kept smiling a sort of bewildered smile.”
“Nothing more?” asked the hoarse voice.
“Nothing more.”
The procurator knocked his cup against the jug as he poured himself wine. When he had drained it to the very bottom, he spoke:
“The matter is this: although we cannot discover—at the present time, at least—any admirers or followers of his, nevertheless one cannot vouch that there are none at all.”
The guest listened attentively, his head inclined.

“And so, to avoid any surprises,” the procurator went on, “I ask you, at once and without any fuss, to remove from the face of the earth the bodies of all three executed men and to bury them in secrecy and in silence, so that neither word nor whisper of them is ever heard again.”
“As you command, hegemon,” said the guest, and he rose, saying: “In view of the difficulty and the responsibility of the matter, permit me to leave at once.”

“No, sit down a while longer,” said Pilate, stopping his guest with a gesture. “There are two more questions. The first: your enormous services in the most difficult of work, as head of the secret service to the procurator of Judea, give me the pleasant opportunity of reporting on them in Rome.”
At this the guest’s face turned pink; he rose and bowed to the procurator, saying:
“I only do my duty in the imperial service!”

“But I would like to ask you,” the hegemon went on, “if you are offered a transfer from here with promotion, to refuse it and remain here. I would not for anything in the world wish to part with you. Let them reward you in some other way.”
“I am happy to serve under your command, hegemon.”
“That pleases me very much. And so, the second question. It concerns that, what’s his name... Judas from Kiriath.”
Here the guest sent the procurator his look and at once, as was proper, extinguished it.
“They say,” the procurator went on, lowering his voice, “that he has supposedly received money for welcoming that mad philosopher so warmly into his house.”
“Will receive,” the head of the secret service quietly corrected Pilate.
“And is the sum large?”
“That no one can know, hegemon.”
“Not even you?” said the hegemon, expressing praise by his astonishment.
“Alas, not even I,” the guest answered calmly. “But that he will receive the money this evening, that I do know. He has been summoned to Caiaphas’s palace tonight.”
“Ah, the greedy old man from Kiriath,” the procurator remarked, smiling. “He is an old man, isn’t he?”
“The procurator is never mistaken, but this time he is,” the guest answered courteously. “The man from Kiriath is a young man.”
“You don’t say! Can you give me a description of him? A fanatic?”
“Oh no, Procurator.”
“I see. And anything else?”
“Very handsome.”
“And what else? Has he, perhaps, some passion?”
“It is hard to know everyone in this enormous city so very precisely, Procurator...”
“Oh no, no, Aphranius! Do not belittle your merits.”
“He has one passion, Procurator.” The guest made a tiny pause. “A passion for money.”
“And what is his occupation?”
Aphranius raised his eyes upward, thought, and answered:
“He works in a money-changer’s shop belonging to one of his relatives.”

“Ah, I see, I see, I see, I see.” Here the procurator fell silent, looked around to see whether there was anyone on the balcony, and then said quietly: “So this is the thing—I received information today that his throat will be cut tonight.”
Here the guest not only darted his look at the procurator but even held it on him a little, and after that he answered:
“You have spoken of me too flatteringly, Procurator. In my opinion I do not deserve your report. I have no such information.”
“You are worthy of the highest reward,” the procurator answered, “but the information exists.”
“May I venture to ask from whom this information comes?”

“Allow me not to say for the present, all the more so since it is chance, obscure and unreliable. But I am obliged to foresee everything. Such is my office, and above all I am obliged to trust my presentiment, for it has never yet deceived me. The information is that one of Ha-Notsri’s secret friends, outraged by this money-changer’s monstrous betrayal, is conspiring with his accomplices to kill him tonight and to slip the money received for the betrayal to the high priest with a note: ‘I return the accursed money.’”
The head of the secret service cast no more of his unexpected looks at the hegemon and went on listening to him with narrowed eyes, while Pilate continued:
“Imagine—will the high priest be pleased to receive such a gift on the night of the feast?”
“Not only will he not be pleased,” the guest answered with a smile, “but I believe, Procurator, it will cause a very great scandal.”
“I am of the same opinion myself. That is why I ask you to take up this matter, that is, to take every measure to protect Judas from Kiriath.”

“The hegemon’s order will be carried out,” Aphranius began, “but I must reassure the hegemon: the villains’ plan is extremely hard to carry out. Only think”—the guest turned around as he spoke, and went on—“to track a man down, cut his throat, find out besides how much he received, and contrive to return the money to Caiaphas, and all in one night? Tonight?”

“And nevertheless his throat will be cut tonight,” Pilate repeated stubbornly. “I have a presentiment, I tell you! It has never once deceived me.” Here a spasm passed over the procurator’s face, and he briefly rubbed his hands.
“As you command,” the guest responded submissively, rose, drew himself up, and suddenly asked sternly: “So his throat will be cut, hegemon?”
“Yes,” Pilate answered, “and all hope rests solely on your diligence, which astonishes everyone.”
The guest adjusted the heavy belt under his cloak and said:
“I have the honor. I wish you health and joy.”
“Ah, yes,” Pilate cried out softly, “why, I had quite forgotten! Why, I owe you money!..”
The guest was astonished.
“Truly, Procurator, you owe me nothing.”
“But of course I do! When I rode into Yershalaim, remember, there was a crowd of beggars... I wanted to throw them some money, and I had none on me, and I took it from you.”
“Oh, Procurator, that is some trifle!”
“A trifle too ought to be remembered.”
Here Pilate turned, lifted the cloak lying on the chair behind him, took a leather bag from under it and held it out to his guest. The guest bowed as he accepted it and hid it under his cloak.

“I expect,” Pilate began, “a report on the burial, and also on this business of Judas from Kiriath, this very night—do you hear, Aphranius, tonight. The guard will be ordered to wake me the moment you appear. I shall be waiting for you.”

“I have the honor,” said the head of the secret service, and, turning, he walked off the balcony. He could be heard crunching across the wet sand of the terrace, then came the knock of his boots on the marble between the lions; then his legs were cut off, then his body, and at last the hood vanished too. Only then did the procurator notice that the sun was gone and dusk had come.

chapters.title: 26. The Burial
paragraphs: Perhaps it was this dusk that caused the procurator’s appearance to change so sharply. He seemed to age before one’s eyes, to grow hunched, and he became uneasy besides. Once he looked around and for some reason started, glancing at the empty chair with the cloak lying over its back. The night of the feast was approaching, the evening shadows were playing their game, and the weary procurator probably imagined that someone was sitting in the empty chair. Giving way to faint-heartedness—he stirred the cloak—the procurator left it alone and began rushing about the balcony, now rubbing his hands, now running up to the table and seizing his cup, now stopping and staring senselessly at the mosaic of the floor, as if trying to read some writing in it.

For the second time that day anguish had come down upon him. Rubbing his temple, in which all that remained of the hellish pain of the morning was a dull, slightly aching memory, the procurator kept straining to understand the cause of the torment in his soul. And he quickly understood it, but tried to deceive himself. It was clear to him that this afternoon he had irretrievably let something slip, and that now he wanted to make up for what he had let slip by some small and paltry and, above all, belated actions. The self-deception lay in the procurator’s trying to persuade himself that these actions, the present ones, the evening ones, were no less important than the morning’s sentence. But the procurator was having very little success at it.

At one of his turns he stopped short and whistled. In answer to the whistle a deep bark thundered in the dusk, and out of the garden onto the balcony bounded a gigantic, sharp-eared dog with a gray coat, in a collar with gilded studs.
“Banga, Banga,” the procurator called weakly.

The dog rose on its hind legs and lowered its front paws onto its master’s shoulders, almost knocking him to the floor, and licked his cheek. The procurator sat down in the chair; Banga, his tongue hanging out, panting rapidly, lay down at his master’s feet, and the joy in the dog’s eyes meant that the storm was over, the only thing in the world the fearless dog was afraid of, and also that he was here again, beside the man he loved, respected and considered the mightiest in the world, the ruler of all men, thanks to whom the dog considered himself too a privileged being, superior and special. But having lain down at his master’s feet, and without even looking at him, but looking out into the darkening garden, the dog understood at once that some misfortune had befallen his master. So he changed his position, got up, came around from the side and laid his front paws and his head on the procurator’s knees, smearing the skirts of his cloak with wet sand. Banga’s actions were probably meant to say that he was comforting his master and was ready to meet misfortune together with him. This he also tried to express in his eyes, which he kept turning sidelong toward his master, and in his alert, pricked-up ears. So the two of them, dog and man, who loved each other, met the night of the feast on the balcony.

At this time the procurator’s guest was very busy. Having left the upper terrace of the garden in front of the balcony, he went down the stairs to the next terrace of the garden, turned right and came out by the barracks that stood within the palace grounds. In these barracks were quartered the two centuries that had come with the procurator to Yershalaim for the feast, and also the procurator’s secret guard, which was commanded by this very guest. The guest spent a short time in the barracks, no more than ten minutes, but when those ten minutes had passed, three carts drove out of the barracks yard, loaded with entrenching tools and a barrel of water. The carts were escorted by fifteen men in gray cloaks, on horseback. Under this escort the carts left the palace grounds by the back gate, turned west, passed out through a gate in the city wall, and went along a path first to the Bethlehem road, then along it northward, reached the crossroads by the Hebron Gate, and then moved along the Jaffa road, by which the procession with the condemned men had passed that afternoon on its way to the execution. By this time it was already dark, and the moon had appeared on the horizon.

Soon after the carts had left with their escort, the procurator’s guest also departed from the palace grounds on horseback, having changed into a dark, worn chiton. The guest headed not out of the city but into it. Some time later he could be seen riding up to the Antonia fortress, which stood to the north and in the immediate vicinity of the great temple. In the fortress too the guest stayed only a very short time, and after that his trail was found in the Lower City, in its crooked and tangled streets. Here the guest arrived riding a mule.

Knowing the city well, the guest easily found the street he needed. It was called the Greek Street, because several Greek shops were located on it, among them one that sold carpets. It was precisely at this shop that the guest stopped his mule, dismounted and tied it to a ring by the gate. The shop was already locked. The guest went in through the wicket next to the shop entrance and found himself in a small square courtyard, lined on three sides with sheds. Turning a corner in the yard, the guest found himself by the stone terrace of a dwelling house, overgrown with ivy, and looked around. Both the little house and the sheds were dark; no lamps had yet been lit. The guest called softly:
“Niza!”

At this call a door creaked, and in the evening half-dark a young woman without a veil appeared on the little terrace. She leaned over the railing of the terrace, peering anxiously, wanting to know who had come. Recognizing the visitor, she smiled at him warmly, nodded her head and waved her hand.
“Are you alone?” Aphranius asked softly in Greek.

“Alone,” the woman on the terrace whispered. “My husband left for Caesarea this morning.” Here the woman glanced back at the door and added in a whisper: “But the maid is at home.” Here she made a gesture that meant “come in.” Aphranius looked around and stepped onto the stone steps. After this both the woman and he disappeared inside the little house.

Aphranius stayed with this woman a very short time indeed—certainly no more than five minutes. After this he left the house and the terrace, pulled his hood lower over his eyes and went out into the street. By this time lamps were already being lit in the houses, the crush on the eve of the feast was still very great, and Aphranius on his mule was lost in the stream of passers-by and riders. Where he went after that is not known to anyone.

As for the woman whom Aphranius had called Niza, once she was left alone she began to change her clothes, and she was in a great hurry. But however hard it was for her to find the things she needed in the dark room, she did not light a lamp and did not call the maid. Only after she was ready and already had a dark veil over her head was her voice heard in the little house:
“If anyone asks for me, say that I have gone visiting Enanta.”
The old maid could be heard grumbling in the darkness:
“To Enanta? Oh, that Enanta! Didn’t your husband forbid you to go to her? She’s a procuress, your Enanta! I’ll tell your husband...”

“Now, now, now, be quiet,” Niza responded, and slipped out of the little house like a shadow. Niza’s sandals tapped across the stone flags of the courtyard. Grumbling, the maid shut the door to the terrace. Niza had left her house.

At that very time, from another lane in the Lower City, a crooked lane that ran down in steps to one of the city pools, out of the wicket gate of an unsightly house that turned its blind side to the lane and its windows to the yard, there came a young man with a neatly trimmed little beard, in a clean white kefi falling to his shoulders, a new festive blue tallif with tassels at the bottom, and brand-new creaking sandals. The handsome, hook-nosed young man, dressed up for the great feast, walked briskly, overtaking passers-by hurrying home to the festive meal, and watched one window after another light up. The young man was taking the road that led past the bazaar to the palace of the high priest Caiaphas, which stood at the foot of the temple hill.
Some time later he could be seen entering the gates of Caiaphas’s courtyard. And some time after that, leaving the courtyard.

After his visit to the palace, where lamps and torches were already blazing and festive bustle was under way, the young man walked still more briskly, still more joyfully, and hurried back to the Lower City. At the very corner where the street poured into the market square, in the seething crush, he was overtaken by a light woman walking with a sort of dancing gait, in a black veil drawn down to her very eyes. As she overtook the handsome young man, this woman for an instant threw her veil back higher and shot a glance in the young man’s direction, but far from slowing her pace she quickened it, as if trying to get away from the man she had overtaken.

The young man not only noticed this woman—no, he recognized her, and having recognized her he started, stopped, looking after her in bewilderment, and at once set off to catch up with her. Nearly knocking down some passer-by with a jug in his hands, the young man caught up with the woman and, breathing heavily with excitement, called to her:
“Niza!”
The woman turned and narrowed her eyes, and her face showed cold annoyance, and she answered dryly in Greek:
“Ah, it’s you, Judas? I didn’t recognize you at first. But that is a good thing. We have a saying that a man who is not recognized will become rich...”
So agitated that his heart began to leap like a bird under a black cloth, Judas asked in a faltering whisper, afraid that passers-by might hear:
“Where are you going, Niza?”
“And why should you know that?” Niza answered, slowing her pace and looking haughtily at Judas.
Then something childish could be heard in Judas’s voice, and he whispered in confusion:
“But how can that be?.. We agreed, didn’t we? I wanted to come to you. You said you would be at home all evening...”

“Ah no, no,” answered Niza, and capriciously pushed out her lower lip, which made Judas think that her face, the most beautiful face he had ever seen in his life, had grown more beautiful still, “I got bored. You people have a feast, but what am I supposed to do? Sit and listen to you sighing on the terrace? And be afraid, besides, that the maid will tell my husband? No, no, so I decided to go out of the city and listen to the nightingales.”
“Out of the city?” asked Judas, at a loss. “Alone?”
“Of course alone,” answered Niza.
“Let me go with you,” Judas begged breathlessly. His thoughts clouded; he forgot everything in the world and looked with pleading eyes into Niza’s eyes, which were blue but now seemed black.
Niza made no answer and quickened her pace.
“Why don’t you say anything, Niza?” Judas asked plaintively, matching his step to hers.
“And won’t I be bored with you?” Niza suddenly asked, and stopped. At this Judas’s thoughts became completely muddled.
“Well, all right,” Niza relented at last, “let’s go.”
“But where, where?”
“Wait... let’s go into this courtyard and arrange it, or else I’m afraid someone I know will see me and then they’ll say I was out on the street with my lover.”
And at that the bazaar no longer held Niza and Judas. They were whispering in the gateway of some courtyard.

“Go to the olive estate,” Niza whispered, drawing her veil down over her eyes and turning away from some man who was coming into the gateway with a bucket, “to Gethsemane, beyond the Kedron, do you understand?”
“Yes, yes, yes.”
“I shall go on ahead,” Niza went on, “but don’t follow at my heels; keep apart from me. I shall go on ahead... When you cross the stream... you know where the grotto is?”
“I know, I know...”

“Go past the olive press, up the hill, and turn toward the grotto. I shall be there. Only don’t you dare come after me right away; have patience, wait here.” And with these words Niza went out of the gateway as if she had never spoken to Judas at all.

Judas stood there alone for some time, trying to gather his scattering thoughts. Among them was the thought of how he would explain his absence from the festive meal with his family. Judas stood and tried to invent some lie, but in his agitation he thought nothing through properly and prepared nothing, and his legs, of their own accord and without his will, carried him out of the gateway.

Now he changed his route; he was no longer making for the Lower City but turned back toward Caiaphas’s palace. The feast had already entered the city. All around Judas, not only were lights sparkling in the windows, but hymns of praise could already be heard. The last latecomers were driving their donkeys, whipping them on, shouting at them. Judas’s legs carried him by themselves, and he did not notice the dreadful mossy towers of the Antonia flying past him; he did not hear the blare of trumpets in the fortress; he paid no attention whatever to the mounted Roman patrol with a torch that flooded his path with an anxious light.

When he had passed the tower, Judas turned and saw that at a dreadful height above the temple two gigantic five-branched candlesticks had been lit. But even these Judas made out only dimly; it seemed to him that ten lamps of unheard-of size had lit up over Yershalaim, vying with the light of the single lamp that was rising higher and higher over Yershalaim—the lamp of the moon.

Now Judas cared about nothing; he was hurrying to the Gethsemane Gate; he wanted to leave the city as soon as he could. At times it seemed to him that ahead of him, among the backs and faces of the passers-by, a small dancing figure flickered, leading him on. But this was an illusion—Judas understood that Niza was well ahead of him. Judas ran past the money-changers’ shops and at last reached the Gethsemane Gate. There, burning with impatience, he was nevertheless forced to wait. Camels were coming into the city, and after them rode in a Syrian military patrol, which Judas cursed in his mind...

But everything comes to an end. The impatient Judas was already outside the city wall. On his left Judas saw a small cemetery and next to it several striped tents of pilgrims. Crossing the dusty road, flooded with moonlight, Judas made for the Kedron stream in order to cross it. The water murmured quietly under Judas’s feet. Leaping from stone to stone, he at last came out on the opposite bank, the Gethsemane side, and saw with great joy that the road below the gardens here was empty. Not far off he could already see the half-ruined gates of the olive estate.

After the stifling city, Judas was struck by the intoxicating smell of the spring night. A wave of scent from the myrtles and acacias of the Gethsemane meadows came pouring over the wall from the garden.

No one was guarding the gates, there was no one in them, and a few minutes later Judas was already running under the mysterious shadow of huge, spreading olive trees. The road led uphill; Judas climbed, breathing heavily, now and then passing out of the darkness onto patterned carpets of moonlight that reminded him of the carpets he had seen in the shop of Niza’s jealous husband. A little later there flashed past on Judas’s left, in a clearing, an olive press with a heavy stone wheel and a pile of barrels of some kind. There was no one in the garden. The work had ended at sunset, and now above Judas choirs of nightingales thundered and trilled.

Judas’s goal was near. He knew that on his right, in the darkness, he would soon begin to hear the quiet whisper of water falling in the grotto. And so it happened: he heard it. It was growing cooler and cooler.
Then he slowed his pace and called softly:
“Niza!”

But instead of Niza, a stocky male figure detached itself from the thick trunk of an olive tree and leapt out onto the road, and something flashed in its hand and at once went out. With a faint cry Judas threw himself back, but a second man barred his way.
The first, the one in front, asked Judas:
“How much did you get just now? Speak, if you want to keep your life!”
Hope flared up in Judas’s heart, and he cried out desperately:
“Thirty tetradrachms! Thirty tetradrachms! All I got is on me. Here is the money! Take it, but give me my life!”

The man in front instantly snatched the purse from Judas’s hands. And at that same moment, behind Judas’s back, a knife flew up and struck the lover like lightning under the shoulder blade. Judas was flung forward, and he threw his hands, with their fingers clawed, up into the air. The man in front caught Judas on his knife and drove it into Judas’s heart up to the hilt.
“Ni... za...” Judas said, not in his own high, clear young voice but in a voice low and reproachful, and he made not another sound. His body struck the ground so hard that it hummed.
Then a third figure appeared on the road. This third man wore a cloak with a hood.

“Don’t dawdle,” he ordered. The killers quickly wrapped the purse in leather together with a note handed to them by the third man, and tied a rope crosswise around it. The second man thrust the bundle inside the front of his clothes, and then both killers rushed off the road in different directions, and the darkness among the olive trees swallowed them. The third man squatted down beside the murdered man and looked into his face. In the shadow it appeared to the onlooker white as chalk and somehow beautiful, as if inspired.

A few seconds later there was no one living on the road. The lifeless body lay with its arms flung wide. The left foot had landed in a patch of moonlight, so that every strap of the sandal could be clearly seen. The whole garden of Gethsemane was ringing with nightingales’ song at that time. Where the two who had cut Judas’s throat went, no one knows, but the route of the third man, the one in the hood, is known. Leaving the path, he plunged into the thicket of olive trees, making his way south. He climbed over the garden wall far from the main gate, in its southern corner, where the top stones of the masonry had fallen out. Soon he was on the bank of the Kedron. Then he went into the water and made his way for some time through the water, until he saw in the distance the silhouettes of two horses and a man beside them. The horses too were standing in the stream. The water flowed, washing around their hooves. The groom mounted one of the horses, the man in the hood leapt onto the other, and slowly the two of them went along in the stream, and the stones could be heard crunching under the horses’ hooves. Then the riders came out of the water, climbed up onto the Yershalaim bank and went at a walk beneath the city wall. Here the groom separated from him, galloped on ahead and disappeared from view, while the man in the hood stopped his horse, dismounted on the deserted road, took off his cloak, turned it inside out, took from under the cloak a flat helmet without plumes and put it on. Now it was a man in a military chlamys, with a short sword at his hip, who leapt onto the horse. He touched the reins, and the hot-blooded cavalry horse set off at a trot, jolting its rider. He had not far to go—the rider was approaching the southern gate of Yershalaim.

Under the arch of the gate the restless flames of torches danced and leapt. Soldiers of the guard from the second century of the Lightning Legion sat on stone benches playing dice. Seeing a military man ride in, the soldiers jumped up from their places; the military man waved to them and rode into the city.

The city was flooded with festive lights. The flames of lamps played in every window, and from everywhere, merging into a discordant choir, came hymns of praise. Glancing now and then into the windows that faced the street, the rider could see people at the festive table, on which lay the meat of a kid, and cups of wine stood among dishes of bitter herbs. Whistling some quiet little tune, the rider made his way at an unhurried trot through the deserted streets of the Lower City toward the Antonia Tower, glancing now and then at the five-branched candlesticks blazing above the temple, such as had never been seen anywhere in the world, or at the moon, which hung higher still than the candlesticks.

The palace of Herod the Great took no part whatever in the celebration of the Passover night. In the auxiliary quarters of the palace, which faced south and where the officers of the Roman cohort and the legate of the legion were lodged, lights were burning, and some movement and life could be sensed there. But the front part, the state part, where the palace’s only and involuntary inhabitant—the procurator—lived, seemed, with all its colonnades and golden statues, to have gone blind under the brilliant moon. Here, inside the palace, darkness and silence reigned. And the procurator, as he had told Aphranius, did not wish to go inside. He ordered a bed to be made up on the balcony, in the same place where he had dined and where in the morning he had conducted the interrogation. The procurator lay down on the couch that had been made ready, but sleep did not wish to come to him. The naked moon hung high in the clear sky, and for several hours the procurator did not take his eyes off it.

At about midnight sleep at last took pity on the hegemon. Yawning convulsively, the procurator unfastened and threw off his cloak, took off the belt that girded his tunic, with a broad steel knife in a sheath, laid it on the chair beside the couch, took off his sandals and stretched out. Banga at once climbed up onto the bed and lay down beside him, head to head, and the procurator, putting his hand on the dog’s neck, at last closed his eyes. Only then did the dog fall asleep too.

The couch was in half-darkness, screened from the moon by a column, but from the steps of the porch a ribbon of moonlight stretched to the bed. And as soon as the procurator lost touch with what was around him in reality, he at once set off along the shining road and went up it, straight to the moon. He even laughed in his sleep from happiness, so wonderfully and so uniquely had everything turned out on the transparent blue road. He walked accompanied by Banga, and beside him walked the wandering philosopher. They were arguing about something very complicated and important, and neither of them could defeat the other. They did not agree with each other on anything, and that made their argument especially interesting and endless. It went without saying that today’s execution had turned out to be the purest misunderstanding—for here, after all, was the philosopher, who had thought up such an incredibly absurd thing as that all people are good, walking beside him, and so he was alive. And of course it would be utterly horrible even to think that such a man could be executed. There had been no execution! There had not! That was the charm of this journey up the stairway of the moon.

There was as much free time as was needed, and the storm would not come until evening, and cowardice was undoubtedly one of the most terrible vices. So said Yeshua Ha-Notsri. No, philosopher, I object: it is the most terrible vice!

Take, for example, the present procurator of Judea, then a tribune in the legion: he was not a coward that time in the Valley of the Maidens, when the furious Germans all but tore Ratslayer the Giant to pieces. But have mercy on me, philosopher! Can you, with your intelligence, really allow the thought that for the sake of a man who has committed a crime against Caesar the procurator of Judea would ruin his career?
“Yes, yes,” Pilate moaned and sobbed in his sleep.

Of course he would ruin it. In the morning he would not yet have ruined it, but now, at night, having weighed everything, he was willing to ruin it. He would do anything to save from execution an utterly innocent, mad dreamer and healer!

“Now we shall always be together,” said the ragged wandering philosopher to him in his sleep, the philosopher who had somehow come to stand in the path of the knight of the golden spear. “Where there is one, there at once the other will be! When they remember me, they will at once remember you too! Me, a foundling, the son of unknown parents, and you, the son of the astrologer king and of the miller’s daughter, the beauty Pila.”

“Yes, see that you don’t forget, remember me, the son of the astrologer,” Pilate begged in his sleep. And having secured in his sleep a nod from the beggar of En-Sarid walking beside him, the cruel procurator of Judea wept and laughed in his sleep for joy.

All this was good, but all the more terrible was the hegemon’s awakening. Banga growled at the moon, and the slippery blue road, as if rolled smooth with oil, gave way beneath the procurator. He opened his eyes, and the first thing he remembered was that the execution had taken place. The first thing the procurator did was to seize Banga’s collar with a habitual gesture; then with sick eyes he began to look for the moon and saw that it had moved a little to one side and turned silvery. Its light was being overpowered by an unpleasant, restless light that played on the balcony right before his eyes. In the hands of the centurion Ratslayer a torch blazed and smoked. The man holding it was glancing sidelong, with fear and spite, at the dangerous beast that was crouching to spring.

“Leave him, Banga,” said the procurator in a sick voice, and coughed. Shielding himself from the flame with his hand, he went on: “Even at night, even by moonlight, I have no peace. O gods! Yours is a bad office too, Mark. You maim soldiers...”
Mark gazed at the procurator in the greatest astonishment, and the procurator came to his senses. To smooth over the needless words he had spoken half asleep, the procurator said:
“Don’t take offense, centurion. My position, I repeat, is worse still. What do you want?”
“The head of the secret guard is here to see you,” Mark reported calmly.

“Call him, call him,” the procurator ordered, clearing his throat with a cough, and began feeling for his sandals with his bare feet. The flame played on the columns, and the centurion’s caligae clattered across the mosaic. The centurion went out into the garden.
“Even by moonlight I have no peace,” the procurator said to himself, grinding his teeth.
In the centurion’s place the man in the hood appeared on the balcony.
“Banga, leave him,” the procurator said quietly, and squeezed the back of the dog’s neck.

Before he began to speak, Aphranius, as was his habit, looked around and stepped into the shadow, and, having made sure that apart from Banga there was no one on the balcony who should not be, said quietly:
“I ask to be put on trial, Procurator. You turned out to be right. I was unable to protect Judas from Kiriath; his throat has been cut. I ask for a trial and dismissal.”
It seemed to Aphranius that four eyes were looking at him—a dog’s and a wolf’s.
Aphranius took from under his chlamys a purse stiff with blood, sealed with two seals.
“This bag of money was thrown into the high priest’s house by the killers. The blood on this bag is the blood of Judas from Kiriath.”
“How much is in it, I wonder?” asked Pilate, bending over the bag.
“Thirty tetradrachms.”
The procurator smirked and said:
“Not much.”
Aphranius was silent.
“Where is the murdered man?”
“That I do not know,” the man who never parted with his hood answered with calm dignity. “This morning we shall begin the search.”
The procurator started, and let go of the sandal strap, which would not fasten.
“But you know for certain that he has been killed?”
To this the procurator received a dry answer:

“I have been at work in Judea for fifteen years, Procurator. I began my service under Valerius Gratus. I do not need to see the corpse in order to say that a man has been killed, and so I report to you that the man called Judas, from the town of Kiriath, had his throat cut several hours ago.”

“Forgive me, Aphranius,” Pilate answered, “I am not properly awake yet, that is why I said it. I sleep badly”—the procurator smiled faintly—“and I keep seeing a moonbeam in my sleep. So funny, imagine. As if I were walking along that beam. And so, I should like to know your conjectures in this matter. Where do you intend to look for him? Sit down, head of the secret service.”
Aphranius bowed, moved a chair closer to the bed and sat down, his sword clanking.
“I intend to look for him not far from the olive press in the garden of Gethsemane.”
“I see, I see. And why there in particular?”
“Hegemon, as I reckon it, Judas was killed neither in Yershalaim itself nor anywhere far from it. He was killed just outside Yershalaim.”
“I consider you one of the outstanding experts in your profession. I do not know, however, how matters stand in Rome, but in the colonies you have no equal. Explain: why?”

“In no case do I admit the thought,” Aphranius said quietly, “that Judas would have let himself fall into the hands of any suspicious people within the city limits. You cannot cut a man’s throat in secret in the street. That means he would have had to be lured into some cellar. But the service has already searched for him in the Lower City and would certainly have found him. But he is not in the city, that I can vouch for. If he had been killed far from the city, this packet of money could not have been thrown in so soon. He was killed near the city. They managed to lure him out of the city.”
“I cannot conceive how that could have been done.”
“Yes, Procurator, that is the hardest question in the whole affair, and I do not even know whether I shall manage to resolve it.”

“Truly, a mystery! On the evening of the feast a believer goes out of the city for no known reason, leaving the Passover meal, and perishes there. Who could have lured him out, and with what? Was it not a woman who did it?” the procurator suddenly asked, inspired.
Aphranius answered calmly and weightily:

“In no case, Procurator. That possibility is entirely excluded. One must reason logically. Who had an interest in Judas’s death? Some wandering dreamers, some circle in which, first of all, there were no women at all. To marry, Procurator, one needs money; to bring a human being into the world one needs the same; but to cut a man’s throat with the help of a woman one needs a very great deal of money, and no vagabonds have it. There was no woman in this business, Procurator. I will say more: such an interpretation of the murder can only put us off the scent, hinder the investigation and confuse me.”
“I see that you are entirely right, Aphranius,” Pilate said, “and I only allowed myself to put forward my conjecture.”
“Alas, it is mistaken, Procurator.”
“But what, then, what?” exclaimed the procurator, peering into Aphranius’s face with greedy curiosity.
“I believe it is still the same money.”
“A remarkable thought! But who could have offered him money at night outside the city, and for what?”

“Oh no, Procurator, not like that. I have one single conjecture, and if it is wrong, then I may well find no other explanation.” Aphranius leaned closer to the procurator and finished in a whisper: “Judas wanted to hide his money in a secluded place known to him alone.”
“A very subtle explanation. That, evidently, is how the matter stood. Now I understand you: it was not people who lured him out, but his own idea. Yes, yes, that is so.”
“Just so. Judas was mistrustful. He hid his money from people.”
“Yes, you said, in Gethsemane. But why you intend to look for him there in particular—that, I confess, I do not understand.”

“Oh, Procurator, that is the simplest thing of all. No one is going to hide money on the roads, in open and empty places. Judas was neither on the road to Hebron nor on the road to Bethany. He had to be in a sheltered, secluded place with trees. It is so simple. And outside Yershalaim there are no other places like that except Gethsemane. He could not have gone far.”
“You have completely convinced me. So what is to be done now?”
“I shall at once begin searching for the killers who tracked Judas outside the city, and meanwhile I myself, as I have already reported to you, shall go on trial.”
“For what?”

“My men lost him in the evening at the bazaar after he left Caiaphas’s palace. How it happened I cannot conceive. Such a thing has never happened before in my life. He was put under observation immediately after our conversation. But in the area of the bazaar he doubled off somewhere, made such a strange loop that he got away without a trace.”

“I see. I declare to you that I do not consider it necessary to put you on trial. You did all you could, and no one in the world”—here the procurator smiled—“could have done more than you! Punish the agents who lost Judas. But here too, I warn you, I should not like the punishment to be in the least severe. After all, we did everything we could to look after that scoundrel! Oh yes, I forgot to ask”—the procurator rubbed his forehead—“how did they manage to throw the money in to Caiaphas?”
“You see, Procurator... It is not especially complicated. The avengers went around the back of Caiaphas’s palace, where the lane overlooks the back yard. They threw the packet over the fence.”
“With a note?”
“Yes, exactly as you supposed, Procurator. But, as a matter of fact—” here Aphranius tore the seal from the packet and showed its inside to Pilate.
“Good gracious, what are you doing, Aphranius? The seals must surely be the temple’s!”
“The procurator need not trouble himself over that question,” Aphranius answered, closing the packet.
“Can it be that you have all the seals?” Pilate asked, laughing.
“It could not be otherwise, Procurator,” Aphranius answered without any laughter, very sternly.
“I can imagine what went on at Caiaphas’s!”
“Yes, Procurator, it caused very great agitation. They invited me immediately.”
Even in the half-dark it could be seen how Pilate’s eyes were flashing.
“That is interesting, interesting...”

“I venture to disagree, Procurator, it was not interesting. A most tedious and tiresome business. When I asked whether any money had been paid out to anyone at Caiaphas’s palace, I was told categorically that it had not.”
“Oh, really? Well, then, if it was not paid out, it was not paid out. All the harder it will be to find the killers.”
“Quite right, Procurator.”
“Yes, Aphranius, here is what has suddenly occurred to me: did he not do away with himself?”
“Oh no, Procurator,” Aphranius answered, even leaning back in his chair in astonishment, “forgive me, but that is entirely improbable!”
“Ah, in this city everything is probable! I am ready to wager that in a very short time rumors of it will be creeping all over the city.”
Here Aphranius darted his look at the procurator, thought, and answered:
“That may be, Procurator.”
The procurator evidently still could not let go of this question of the murder of the man from Kiriath, though everything was already clear, and he even said with a certain dreaminess:
“And I should have liked to see how they killed him.”
“He was killed with extraordinary skill, Procurator,” Aphranius answered, glancing at the procurator with a certain irony.
“And how do you know that?”
“Be so good as to look at the bag, Procurator,” Aphranius answered. “I vouch to you that Judas’s blood gushed out in a wave. I have seen murdered men in my time, Procurator!”
“So he will certainly not rise again?”
“No, Procurator, he will rise,” Aphranius answered, smiling philosophically, “when the trumpet of the Messiah whom they expect here sounds over him. But not before.”
“Enough, Aphranius! That question is clear. Let us turn to the burial.”
“The executed men have been buried, Procurator.”
“Oh, Aphranius, it would be a crime to put you on trial. You are worthy of the highest reward. How did it go?”

Aphranius began his account and related that, while he himself had been occupied with the Judas affair, a detachment of the secret guard, led by his assistant, had reached the hill as evening fell. They had not found one of the bodies on the top. Pilate started and said hoarsely:
“Ah, how did I not foresee that!”
“There is no need to worry, Procurator,” said Aphranius, and went on with his narrative.

The bodies of Dismas and Gestas, their eyes pecked out by birds of prey, had been taken up, and at once the men had rushed off to search for the third body. It was discovered very quickly. A certain man...
“Levi Matvei,” said Pilate, not as a question but rather as a statement.
“Yes, Procurator...”

Levi Matvei had been hiding in a cave on the northern slope of the Bald Skull, waiting for darkness. The naked body of Yeshua Ha-Notsri was with him. When the guards entered the cave with a torch, Levi fell into despair and rage. He shouted that he had committed no crime and that every man, according to the law, had the right to bury an executed criminal if he wished. Levi Matvei said that he did not want to part with this body. He was agitated, shouted something incoherent, now begged, now threatened and cursed...
“Did he have to be seized?” Pilate asked grimly.
“No, Procurator, no,” Aphranius answered very soothingly. “We managed to calm the insolent madman by explaining that the body would be buried.”

Levi, having grasped what had been said, quieted down, but declared that he would not go anywhere and wished to take part in the burial. He said that he would not leave even if they began to kill him, and even offered for that purpose a bread knife he had with him.
“Was he driven off?” Pilate asked in a strangled voice.
“No, Procurator, no. My assistant allowed him to take part in the burial.”
“Which of your assistants was in charge of this?” asked Pilate.
“Tolmai,” Aphranius answered, and added in alarm: “Perhaps he made a mistake?”
“Go on,” Pilate answered, “there was no mistake. I am beginning, in general, to feel a little at a loss, Aphranius; I am evidently dealing with a man who never makes mistakes. That man is you.”

Levi Matvei had been taken into the cart together with the bodies of the executed men, and some two hours later they had reached a deserted ravine to the north of Yershalaim. There the detachment, working in shifts, had dug a deep pit within an hour and buried all three executed men in it.
“Naked?”

“No, Procurator—the detachment had taken chitons with them for the purpose. Rings were put on the fingers of the buried men. Yeshua’s with one notch, Dismas’s with two and Gestas’s with three. The pit has been closed and heaped with stones. Tolmai knows the identifying mark.”
“Ah, if only I could have foreseen it!” Pilate began, wincing. “I ought to have seen this Levi Matvei, you know...”
“He is here, Procurator.”
Pilate, his eyes opened wide, gazed at Aphranius for some time, and then said this:

“I thank you for all that has been done in this matter. Please send Tolmai to me tomorrow, and tell him beforehand that I am pleased with him; and you, Aphranius”—here the procurator took a ring from the pocket of the belt lying on the table and handed it to the head of the secret service—“I ask you to accept this as a keepsake.”
Aphranius bowed and said:
“A great honor, Procurator.”
“Please give rewards to the detachment that carried out the burial. A reprimand to the agents who lost Judas. And Levi Matvei to me at once. I need details of the Yeshua case.”
“As you command, Procurator,” Aphranius responded, and began backing away and bowing, while the procurator clapped his hands and shouted:
“To me, here! A lamp in the colonnade!”

Aphranius was already going off into the garden, and behind Pilate’s back lights were already flickering in the servants’ hands. Three lamps stood on the table before the procurator, and the moonlit night at once retreated into the garden, as if Aphranius had taken it away with him. In Aphranius’s place an unknown small, gaunt man stepped onto the balcony beside the gigantic centurion. The latter, catching the procurator’s eye, at once withdrew into the garden and vanished.

The procurator studied the newcomer with greedy and slightly frightened eyes. So one looks at someone of whom one has heard a great deal, about whom one has thought a great deal oneself, and who has at last appeared.

The man who had come, close to forty, was dark, ragged, covered in dried mud, and he looked out like a wolf, from under his brows. In a word, he was very unsightly and most of all resembled one of the city beggars who jostle in great numbers on the terraces of the temple or in the bazaars of the noisy and dirty Lower City.

The silence lasted a long time, and it was broken by the strange behavior of the man brought to Pilate. His face changed, he swayed, and if he had not caught hold of the edge of the table with a dirty hand he would have fallen.
“What is the matter with you?” Pilate asked him.
“Nothing,” Levi Matvei answered, and made a movement as if he were swallowing something. His thin, bare, dirty neck swelled and fell again.
“What is the matter with you? Answer,” Pilate repeated.
“I am tired,” Levi answered, and looked grimly at the floor.
“Sit down,” said Pilate, and pointed to the chair.
Levi looked mistrustfully at the procurator, moved toward the chair, glanced fearfully at its gold arms, and sat down not in the chair but beside it, on the floor.
“Explain: why did you not sit in the chair?” Pilate asked.
“I am dirty, I would soil it,” said Levi, looking at the ground.
“You will be given something to eat shortly.”
“I don’t want to eat,” Levi answered.
“Why lie?” Pilate asked quietly. “You have not eaten all day, after all, and perhaps longer. Well, all right, don’t eat. I summoned you so that you could show me the knife you had with you.”
“The soldiers took it from me when they brought me in here,” Levi answered, and added grimly: “Give it back to me, I have to return it to its owner, I stole it.”
“What for?”
“To cut the ropes,” Levi answered.
“Mark!” the procurator called, and the centurion stepped in under the columns. “Give me his knife.”
The centurion took a dirty bread knife from one of the two sheaths on his belt and handed it to the procurator, and then withdrew.
“And whom did you take the knife from?”
“From the bread shop by the Hebron Gate, as you come into the city, straight away on the left.”
Pilate looked at the broad blade, tested with his finger, for some reason, whether the knife was sharp, and said:
“Don’t worry about the knife; the knife will be returned to the shop. And now I need a second thing: show me the scroll you carry with you, in which the words of Yeshua are written down.”
Levi looked at Pilate with hatred and smiled such an unkind smile that his face was utterly disfigured.
“You want to take everything away? Even the last thing I have?” he asked.
“I did not tell you, give it to me,” Pilate answered. “I said, show it to me.”

Levi rummaged inside the front of his clothes and took out a roll of parchment. Pilate took it, unrolled it, spread it out between the lights and, squinting, began to study the barely legible ink marks. It was hard to understand these crooked lines, and Pilate frowned and bent down to the very parchment, running his finger along the lines. He did manage to make out, however, that what was written down was a disconnected chain of sayings of some sort, of some dates, household notes and poetic fragments. Some of it Pilate read: “There is no death... Yesterday we ate sweet spring bakkurot...”
Grimacing with the strain, Pilate squinted and read: “We shall see the pure river of the water of life... Mankind will look at the sun through transparent crystal...”
Here Pilate started. In the last lines of the parchment he made out the words: “...greater vice... cowardice.”
Pilate rolled up the parchment and with an abrupt movement handed it to Levi.

“Take it,” he said, and after a silence he added: “You are, I see, a man of books, and there is no reason for you, a lone man, to go about in beggar’s clothes without a roof over your head. I have a large library in Caesarea; I am very rich and want to take you into my service. You will sort and look after the papyri; you will be fed and clothed.”
Levi stood up and answered:
“No, I don’t want to.”
“Why?” the procurator asked, his face darkening. “Do you find me unpleasant? Are you afraid of me?”
The same bad smile distorted Levi’s face, and he said:
“No, because you will be afraid of me. It will not be very easy for you to look me in the face after you have killed him.”
“Be quiet,” Pilate answered. “Take some money.”
Levi shook his head, and the procurator went on:

“You consider yourself, I know, a disciple of Yeshua, but I tell you that you have learned nothing of what he taught you. For if that were so, you would certainly take something from me. Bear in mind that before his death he said that he blamed no one.” Pilate raised a finger meaningfully; Pilate’s face was twitching. “And he himself would certainly have taken something. You are cruel, and he was not cruel. Where will you go?”
Levi suddenly came up to the table, leaned on it with both hands and, looking at the procurator with burning eyes, whispered to him:
“Know this, hegemon: I am going to cut a man’s throat in Yershalaim. I want to tell you this so that you know there will be more blood.”
“I too know that there will be more,” Pilate answered. “You have not surprised me with your words. You want to cut my throat, of course?”

“I shall not manage to cut your throat,” Levi answered, baring his teeth and smiling. “I am not such a fool as to count on that. But I shall cut the throat of Judas from Kiriath; I shall devote the rest of my life to it.”
Here delight showed in the procurator’s eyes, and, beckoning Levi Matvei closer with his finger, he said:
“You will not manage to do that; don’t trouble yourself. Judas’s throat was cut this very night.”
Levi sprang back from the table, looking around wildly, and cried out:
“Who did it?”
“Don’t be jealous,” Pilate answered, baring his teeth, and rubbed his hands. “I am afraid he had admirers besides you.”
“Who did it?” Levi repeated in a whisper.
Pilate answered him:
“I did it.”
Levi opened his mouth and stared at the procurator, and the procurator said quietly:
“It is not much that has been done, of course, but still it was I who did it.” And he added: “Well, and now will you take something?”
Levi thought, softened, and at last said:
“Have them give me a piece of clean parchment.”

An hour passed. Levi was no longer in the palace. Now the silence of the dawn was broken only by the quiet sound of the sentries’ footsteps in the garden. The moon was fading fast; on the other edge of the sky the whitish speck of the morning star could be seen. The lamps had gone out long ago. The procurator lay on the couch. With his hand under his cheek, he was asleep, breathing soundlessly. Beside him slept Banga.
Thus did the fifth procurator of Judea, Pontius Pilate, meet the dawn of the fifteenth of Nisan.
